Last week, I shared my criticism of some aspects of the development sector in two posts —

The Development Sector Needs a Higher Standard. Not a Lower One.

A question I am sometimes asked is why I hold the development sector to a standard I do not apply to the business world. The answer rests on a single, uncomfortable fact: in business, the people whose money is being spent have agency. In the development sector, they do not.

Markets, over time, punish poor capital discipline. In the development sector, the logic is inverted. The TB patient cannot fire the globe-trotting consultant. The smallholder farmer cannot question the panel debating her livelihood. The forest cannot seek a refund from a carbon credit peddler. This is not a minor distinction. It is a moral asymmetry of the first order.

And yet the waste has not merely persisted. It has been institutionalised.
The elite nonprofit complex is now a recognisable feature of the landscape: well-resourced organisations in premium offices, generously compensated executives, a packed calendar of convenings and summits, and alongside them, a consulting industry that does not merely serve the sector but actively shapes its language, its frameworks, and its definition of credibility. These firms are paid by the same organisations whose strategies they assess. The incentive, therefore, is never to disrupt. It is to validate, to elaborate, and to return next year. The result is a closed loop of institutional comfort dressed in the vocabulary of transformation.

I am not arguing that the business world is above critique. It externalises vast social and environmental costs that never appear on a balance sheet. But within its own internal logic, it at least has mechanisms that correct for waste. The development sector has none. Which is precisely why those of us who work within it carry a higher obligation — to insist on rigour, to challenge performative activity, and to refuse the comfortable consensus that good intentions are a substitute for results. The cost of our self-indulgence is paid in the lives of people and the planet.

The development sector exists because the market failed the people it serves. That is not a reason to hold it to a lower standard than the world it critiques. It is the most compelling reason imaginable to hold it to a higher one.

COVID-19 taught us that the world can mobilise extraordinary resources when confronted with an existential threat. Climate change is teaching us that not every existential threat produces the same urgency. 

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗹𝗶𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗸.

COVID-19 was never democratic in its consequences. The poor and vulnerable suffered disproportionately. But the virus could reach the boardroom as easily as the slum or the farm. Wealth and power offered protection, not immunity.

Climate change is different. Its earliest and harshest consequences fall on those who contributed least to the problem and have the fewest means to protect themselves. A farmer cannot move agriculture indoors. A construction worker cannot air-condition a building site. A poor household cannot insure itself against every disaster and failed harvest. Those with wealth and power, meanwhile, can buy themselves protection and, more importantly, time.

Urgency and resource allocation often reflect the exposure and priorities of the powerful, rather than the scale of suffering.

There are other explanations, of course. COVID was immediate and visible. Climate risks accumulate over decades, even as their consequences are already devastating lives and livelihoods. 

Risk is not just a scientific probability. It is also a political variable, shaped by who is exposed, who can escape, who can afford protection and who has the power to demand action.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗸𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗳𝘂𝗹, 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗲𝘀. 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘆 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗹𝗲𝘀𝘀, 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗲𝘀. 𝗘𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲𝘀. 𝗗𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗲𝘀 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗽𝗮𝗻𝗲𝗹𝘀, 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀, 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀, 𝗽𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀, 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗿𝘀, 𝗰𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗯𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀.

Which raises an uncomfortable question:

𝗪𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗹𝗱 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗖𝗢𝗩𝗜𝗗-𝟭𝟵 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝘂𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗶𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘃𝗶𝗿𝘂𝘀 𝗵𝗮𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝘀𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗵𝗼𝗹𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗳𝗮𝗿𝗺𝗲𝗿𝘀, 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗹 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻 𝘀𝗹𝘂𝗺𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗲𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗵𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗳𝘂𝗹 𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗼𝘂𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗱?

The obstacle to climate action is not that we fail to understand the risk or communicate it. It is that those who allocate resources can afford to postpone its consequences.

#ClimateChange #SkinInTheGame #AsymmetryInNarratives

PS: I am acutely aware of my own privilege. I can afford almost everything needed to protect myself from the worst consequences of climate change. And I will probably be dead long before the world reaches net zero. That, perhaps, is precisely the problem. I have the luxury of time. Billions do not.

What would it take to enable more dignified livelihoods for India’s waste pickers?

The circular economy is often discussed in terms of how resources can be reduced, reused, recycled and recovered. But if systems are being rebuilt to value materials differently, there is also a need to rethink how the people who collect, sort, recover and transform those materials are valued.

Waste pickers form the invisible backbone of India’s waste management system. Yet the recognition, security and dignity that should come with this work are often missing. A start-up, with the right support, can create formal employment, giving people greater agency, stability, and the opportunity to define their own economic futures.

A scientific breakthrough is only one part of the innovation journey. Finding its applications, identifying the right markets and building the partnerships to take it forward are equally important.

Venture Center, through TechEx.in and the Centre of Excellence for Clean Energy and Green Hydrogen, hosted the 20th talk in the NCL Innovations Seminar Series featuring Prof. Elicia Maine, W.J. VanDusen Professor of Innovation and Entrepreneurship and Associate Vice-President of Innovation at Simon Fraser University, Canada. Her talk, Technology–Market Matching for Deep Tech Innovation, explored how research discoveries can evolve into commercial ventures.

One example was Ionomr Innovations, founded by Dr. Steven Holdcroft, Dr. Benjamin Britton, Dr. Timothy Peckham and Dr. Titichai Navessin. Emerging from research at Simon Fraser University's Holdcroft Lab, the company developed advanced ion-exchange polymers and membranes for applications including hydrogen fuel cells and electrolysers.

Drawing on economist Christopher Freeman's The Economics of Industrial Innovation, Prof. Maine explored the scissors analogy to explain the two sides of innovation: the recognition of a market need and the development of technological capabilities to address it. Like the two blades of a pair of scissors, neither can create value independently. It is their alignment, and the synchronisation of technological development with market requirements, that makes innovation possible. A promising technology must find an application where its capabilities are valued, while market opportunities must be matched by technologies that can deliver on their requirements.
In her concluding recommendations, Prof. Maine emphasised early technology–market matching, exploring a breadth of target markets, leveraging innovative accelerators and non-dilutive funding, using alliance partners to access markets and research resources, pursuing opportunities in emerging markets, forward integration into industry value chains and maintaining flexible strategies.

The session offered researchers and deep-tech entrepreneurs valuable perspectives on navigating the journey from scientific discovery to commercial impact.
